title: Between two teachers
hook: Epictetus the freed slave, Seneca the rich courtier: one school, two lives

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the jar: thrift at the bottom comes too late. Your line was hold every hour.

Two men, decades apart, belonged to the same school of thought. One began life in chains. The other ended up in a senator's toga. One owned almost nothing; the other owned so much that his enemies made it a weapon against him. This year has given about a hundred days to Epictetus and about ninety to Seneca. Tomorrow opens the notebook of an emperor who learned from both. So today, the last day of Seneca's season, the two stand side by side.
screen: `ONE IN CHAINS, ONE IN A TOGA.` → `A HUNDRED DAYS, AND NINETY.` → `BETWEEN TWO TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: First, Epictetus. Ancient sources say he was born a slave in Hierapolis, in what's now Turkey, and that in Rome he belonged to Epaphroditus, a freed slave who served Nero. He was lame; the sources disagree about why. Once freed, he taught philosophy until the emperor Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome, then taught in Nicopolis, in Greece, for the rest of his life. He wrote nothing. His student Arrian took notes, and that's the handbook you read. Second, Seneca. Born in Córdoba, in Spain, into a wealthy family: a senator, a famous writer, exiled, recalled, tutor and adviser to Nero, and very rich. He wrote shelves of books himself. Third, the overlap. For a while both lived in Rome at the same time, both near Nero's court. There's no evidence they ever met, and nothing in what survives of Epictetus mentions Seneca by name. Fourth, one school, two voices. Epictetus teaches from the front of the room: blunt, demanding, funny, sure. Some things are up to us, and some are not; learn the difference. Seneca writes from the seat beside you, confessing, circling back, admitting he's still learning. Yet side by side, their lessons land on the same few things. What's truly ours is our judgment. Time and life are on loan. Rehearse losing them, and you'll hold them better. A slave and a millionaire, from opposite ends of Roman life, reached the same short list. That doesn't prove the list. But it's worth noticing, and it's why both are worth keeping.
screen: `EPICTETUS: BORN A SLAVE, WROTE NOTHING.` · `SENECA: RICH, AND WROTE SHELVES.` · `SAME CITY, NO SIGN THEY MET.` · `TWO VOICES, ONE SHORT LIST.` · then, large: `TWO TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Picture Epictetus at the front of a small room in Nicopolis, leaning on his stick, and let one thing he taught you this year come back. Then picture Seneca at his desk, writing to a friend, and find one thing from him. Hold the two side by side for a few breaths.
Arrian. The student who took notes on Epictetus's teaching, since Epictetus himself wrote nothing: the source of the handbook you read. Today's word.
Your line: two teachers. The blunt one at the front, and the friend in the next seat. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism today read Epictetus and Seneca side by side, turning to the handbook for its clear rules and to the letters for their companionship.

fork.setup: Domitian expels the philosophers from Rome. you're Epictetus, a freed man with a bad leg and no fortune. what do you do?
options: stop teaching and stay quietly in Rome.
move to Nicopolis in Greece and teach there.
write a book defending philosophy to the emperor.
fork.reveal: he went to Nicopolis and taught for the rest of his life. the students kept coming, Arrian among them.

original.note: Greek: a porch, a colonnade. The Painted Porch in Athens, where Zeno taught, gave the Stoics their name.

trapdoor: what you thought: two old philosophers who said the same things.
what it means: a freed slave and a rich courtier, from opposite ends of Rome, reaching the same short list.
what a scholar hears: both are 'late Stoics', long after Zeno; the early Stoics' books survive only in fragments, so whole Stoic books reach us mainly through them and Marcus.

chat.says: Did Epictetus write that handbook himself?
options: No, he wrote nothing. His student Arrian took notes, and those became the handbook.
Yes, he wrote it in Rome while he was still a slave of Epaphroditus.
No, Seneca wrote it down for him after they met at Nero's court.
chat.meaning: Epictetus wrote nothing. His student Arrian took notes, and that's the handbook. There's no evidence he and Seneca ever met.

Epictetus.meaning: a Stoic teacher, born a slave, who wrote nothing himself

Hierapolis.meaning: Epictetus's birthplace, in what's now Turkey

Epaphroditus.meaning: a freed slave who served Nero and owned Epictetus

Domitian.meaning: the emperor who expelled philosophers from Rome

Nicopolis.meaning: a town in Greece where Epictetus taught for the rest of his life

Epictetus: born c. AD 50 in Hierapolis, Phrygia; slave of Epaphroditus (Nero's freedman secretary); lame (Celsus/Origen story vs. Simplicius' rheumatism); expelled under Domitian (c. AD 93–95; Aulus Gellius 15.11 records the expulsion) and taught at Nicopolis. Confirm.
'Nothing in what survives of Epictetus mentions Seneca by name': confirm.
Seneca born in Corduba (Córdoba) c. 4 BC–AD 1; confirm.
